We never reached the far wall that summer, though Dario spoke of it each morning as if distance were only another word to learn. He sat on the rim of the salt pool in Havana, trousers rolled, and named things in the language of his village: tile, gull, the green rust on the ladder. Bartolo repeated each word and swam a length before the next. On Thursday she stopped short of the far wall, held the rope, and came back saying she had only wanted to rest. Dario nodded and gave her the word for rest, then a second, older word that he said meant resting before one has finished. She practiced it without asking why. Later, reciting the colors, he paused at the word for the rust, and let her supply it, which she did loudly, as though he had been testing her. On the walk home she carried his towel over her shoulder, still damp at one corner where the rope had dripped on it.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the passage?

Once, near the end of my nights at the pharmacy in Lima, Valentina came in at two in the morning and did not ask for anything on the shelves. For six years she had sent me her chapters typed, never handwritten; the notebooks she kept locked in a drawer her own sister had never seen. That week a colleague had told me, kindly and wrongly, that Valentina was talking to a translator in Madrid. I said as much while I rang up the mints she finally chose. She looked at the fluorescent tubes and remarked that they made everyone look like a ghost of themselves. Then she set a green notebook on the counter, its pages crowded with her slanted ink and crossed-out lines, and said she would collect it Thursday. I put it under the register, beside the night ledger, and kept my hand on its cover until the bell over the door stopped swinging.

Flour dusted my stepmother's wrists before the sun was up, and by five she had already shaped forty loaves for an oven she could no longer afford to repair. I was sixteen and had told her, more than once, that the bakery in our Tbilisi lane was finished: the new supermarket sold bread cheaper, and Stanislav, who had fired the oven for my father, was nearly eighty. She never argued. She only set out cups of tea each morning, one for herself and one for Stanislav, and a third, untouched, at my place on the bench. __One morning I sat down and drank it, and she slid the scoring blade across the table toward me without a word.__ I cut the loaves badly. Stanislav laughed until he coughed. Dmitri, my friend from school, asked that afternoon why my hands smelled of yeast, and I told him I was only helping until the place closed. I said that for eleven more years.

Who tells a dying man that the salt works he built will be sold by spring? I asked Armand this on my third week, while we raked the evaporation pans outside Beirut and the crust cracked white under our boots. He did not answer. He told me instead to rake slower, so the crystals would not cloud. That evening we carried a tin of the first harvest to Giada's bed, and Armand described the pans to him in detail: how high the brine stood, how the wind had come off the sea. Every word was true. He left out only the letter from the buyers, folded in his breast pocket. Driving back, I said that wasn't lying, exactly. Armand turned the radio up. I have spent years since retelling that drive, and I always slow down at the part where he raked so carefully for a man who would never see the sale.

When Anacleto came up to the terrace on Thursdays, he brought his grammar and, without fail, a small paper of coffee, which he set on the wall beside my inkstand as though it had arrived there by itself. I never thanked him, and he never waited to be thanked. We read our verbs while the bay below us went from grey to silver. Some months before, I had paid the physician who attended his father, and neither of us had spoken of it since; I believed the matter forgotten, as I had wished it to be. This Thursday, however, he recited the conditional mood without a single error and then asked, quite formally, whether I might set him harder lessons, longer ones, as many as I pleased. Rosalinda, my housekeeper, laughed from the doorway at such appetite. I did not laugh. I looked at the coffee on the wall, and then at his careful hands, which had already opened the grammar to a page we had not reached.

On Monday, when I stopped for my mother's mackerel, he wrapped it in a page of newspaper and asked whether the dictionary was heavy. I said it was. He nodded, satisfied, and charged me the usual price, and for years I let my own children believe I had won that contest fair.

By seven the gym on Seventy-First smells of floor wax
and the folding chairs are already crooked.
Devon, who rode my father's ferry every summer
and talked the whole way across about nothing,
asks me to the spring dance under the dead scoreboard.
I tell him he dances like a dropped mop.
I tell him I have a shift on the dock,
which is not lying, exactly—
my father would let me off if I asked.
He laughs. He says, Kenya, fair enough,
and goes out whistling through the side door.
I stack the chairs he knocked over
and straighten the ones he didn't,
and when the custodian kills the lights
I stand a while by the bleachers
where he left his jacket, and fold it
sleeve over sleeve, collar up,
and carry it home on the ferry, on my lap,
the whole way across, saying nothing.

I wrote in my notebook that he talked as a gull walks, much and to no end, and showed the line to the clerk, who laughed. I was not mocking him, exactly, or not only. On the second morning the porter offered me the ladies' waiting room, which was quiet and warm, and I said I preferred the draught. For two years I took the same stool at the stall, the one that faced away from the church of my childhood, and Father Bao, who still ate there before morning Mass, took the stool beside the pot. We nodded and did not speak. In March a notice went up on the church gate: he would be sent north after Easter. The following Monday I came twenty minutes earlier than usual. I ordered two bowls, paid for both, and left his with the cook, covered with a saucer to keep the steam in. I did this every morning for three weeks. I did not once go through the gate. On his final morning I turned my stool around, so that it faced the church, and sat there until he came.

Stanislav had kept that book for the old owner of the house on the hill for thirty-one seasons, writing each planting in a narrow hand and heading every page with the owner's initials, as he had been taught. Three rules governed the reading room on the second floor: no food, no phones, no voices above a whisper. Jonas kept all three, and when he needed Yusuf's attention he touched the edge of the table and murmured Ustaz, as he had since their first rehearsal eight years before, though Yusuf was barely older. They came most afternoons to copy out parts, the oud case propped between their chairs. That Thursday an envelope slid from the case's lid pocket: a festival in Lyon, addressed to Yusuf alone, offering a solo evening and a fee for one. Jonas read it, folded it along its creases, and returned it to the pocket. He said nothing. At four, the hour they usually packed up together, he copied out his own part of their new piece twice, left one copy on Yusuf's side of the table with the tempo markings filled in, and walked down the stairs ahead of him.

Remedios took the loose strands from him, tucked the next three herself, crookedly, and he let the crooked ones stand.

You carried it off Matteo's freighter four years ago, coiled around a bundle of clothes, when the captain found you behind the rice sacks and, instead of calling the harbor police, brought you here. In the workshop the rope is useful. You tie finished stacks of ledgers with it for delivery, then untie it and coil it again by your bench, always beside the cloth bundle you never quite unpack. Matteo, who binds books now instead of sailing, has stopped asking about the bundle. This year he taught you headbands, the small stitched cords at the top of a spine. On Friday you take the rope, unpick it strand by strand, and sew the strands into the headband of a ledger for the harbor office. Then you shake the bundle open, Putri, and fold your shirts into the drawer under the bench.

Years later, Dmitri would remember the cellar in Tbilisi by its smell of wet paper. The author's manuscripts had been stored there in tin trunks, and when the spring flood came he waded down beside her with a lamp, reading each label aloud: chapter four, the letters, the second draft of the novel he had spent two winters translating. The house rule, set by the landlord Anselm, was that no tenant might run the pump; one waited for Anselm, who was rarely home. The author repeated the rule courteously, thanked Dmitri for his patience, and asked whether he would mind holding the lamp a little higher. He minded nothing. He held it higher. Water reached the second strap of the trunks. Dmitri said, very politely, that he would wait upstairs for the landlord. He climbed the steps, set the lamp on the landing, and went out by the yard door, toward the pump shed.

Once, at dusk, I walked the soccer field in Bologna
with Ottavio, who had clerked for me the final year
before they took my robe and gave me a garden.
Still he called me Judge Fiorella, and still he carried
my late husband's whistle, the silver one,
polished and wrapped in a folded handkerchief,
and spoke of it as evidence: its dent, its chain,
the date engraved in letters small as rulings.
I answered him as I once answered counsel,
with thanks, with patience, with the proper phrases,
and asked him kindly if he meant to keep it.
He said it was mine.
The field was empty.
Lights came on.
A boy's ball rolled to the line and stopped.
I thanked him for his care.
I took the whistle from the cloth
and, still thanking him, blew it once
and sent the ball back to the boy.

Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?

Harvest makes fools of everyone. Dolores had said so for thirty seasons, and this year she said it chiefly about Esteban. Since the pickers she had trained without him had filled more baskets than any crew in Seville, the young man had taken to sulking beneath the olive tree at the end of the rows, as idle and decorative, she told the foreman, as a weathervane on a windless day. She complained of his boots, of his singing, of the way he still walked as if the whole slope belonged to him. She did not want him back on the crew; no, that was not quite it, either. Each evening, when the carts went down to the press, she counted the baskets aloud and paused at the blank space on the tally board where his name had once been chalked. On the last morning she rose before the others, walked the steep row he had always claimed, and left those vines unpicked until he came down from the tree.

problem.passage:
Why did Hedwig wind the clocks backward? Kalani, the landlord's son, had noticed it on three rent days running: while her father counted coins at the bench of the little Havana shop, she moved along the wall of clocks and turned each key the wrong way, gently, until it resisted, and then let it go. He took it for a girl's idle mischief and said nothing, since his own father disliked complaints. On the fourth rent day his father asked to see the shop's account book. Hedwig's father went pale and reached for the drawer, but Hedwig was quicker; she set the book on the counter herself, opened to a page in her own neat hand, and stepped back to the clocks. Kalani, reading over his father's shoulder, saw that every entry was dated a week before the coins had truly come in. His father nodded and closed the book. Hedwig turned one more key the wrong way and looked at Kalani, and he held her gaze without a word.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

Taeyang did not look at it. __He had folded the corner of every map he owned toward the north, a habit I took for the neatness of a clerk.__ Outside, a cart of melons rolled past the little post office, and the clerk inside weighed our parcel twice, frowning at the scale as though it had insulted him. Then he handed the map back to me and asked whether the river road was paved.

Three rules governed the chess club on the promenade, and Radek had written them himself on a card above the door: no talking during play, no coffee near the boards, no lessons for another member's pupils. __Vesna kept her own clock in a velvet bag, though the club had owned electric ones for twenty years.__ That afternoon the wind off the water rattled the windows, and two old men argued about whether the gulls were louder this year. Radek's pupil, a boy of eleven, sat across from him practicing the sealed move, the old custom of writing a move in an envelope when a game is paused overnight. Hardly anyone under sixty in the club still knew how to do it properly. The boy kept forgetting to stop the clock before he wrote. At six, Vesna rose, crossed to Radek's table, and set the velvet bag beside the envelope. She left without a word. Inside was her clock, its two buttons worn pale, with a slip of paper wedged under the stop lever.

"Your tomatoes are leaning again," Hana called across the fence, and I pretended not to hear her. Twenty years ago we had shared a stage in Bologna, she the soprano everyone remembered and I the mezzo who sang the second verse. Four things Ama demanded of an apprentice: sharp chisels, swept floors, silence while she measured, and one finished piece before the passes opened. That winter the snow shut us into the cabin above the valley outside Lima for nine days. Each morning Ama took a small photograph from her coat, glanced at it, and slid it face down beneath the glue pot. On the third day she told me to build a frame of cedar, five inches by seven. Wanjiru, its captain, found the stowaway behind the brine barrels: a girl of perhaps sixteen named Solange, who said she had run from a boarding school and had a little brother waiting at the far landing. The truth would frighten him; a lie would have to be kept up for years. Wanjiru, who had once told her own sister that their father was merely 'at sea,' found that she had opinions. By the time the barge floated free at dusk, the two of them had written three versions of the story on the back of a cargo manifest, and crossed out every one.

I boarded Albert's barge on the Irwell expecting to stay ten minutes. Thirty years earlier he had torn my essay in half before the whole class, and I had carried that sound with me ever since. Now he moved slowly between coils of rope, offering tea in a chipped mug, and I kept my coat buttoned and my answers short. He did not apologize. Instead he showed me a shoebox of student papers he had kept, and mine was near the top, taped carefully along its tear. I set the mug down without drinking. Still, when he struggled with the stove, I reached over and lit it for him, and I did not leave when the ten minutes were up. Gulls settled on the roof of the cabin, and the water knocked against the hull.

Tonight, though, he slid the envelope across the crate between them and tapped one line with a tar-stained finger. Read only this part, he said. Rania bent over the paper, sounding out each syllable. Smoke from the tandoor and the sour breath of rising dough met me each morning in our Samarkand bakery, long before the shutters opened. Darius came at four, though I paid him from six. I never asked him to come early, and he never asked to be paid for it. My husband, before he died, had lent the boy's mother money for a surgery; the ledger with her name in it still sat on the shelf above the flour bins. Darius dusted that shelf every morning and never once touched the ledger. On the coldest days I burned the stale loaves in the oven and told him there was no bread to spare, then left a warm round on the stool by the door, where he would find it without having to thank me. Outside, a cart rattled over the stones toward the market.

On his last night he asked only whether I had kept them, and when I said yes, all nineteen, he closed his eyes and smiled. I left the cranes on my windowsill for years, where they faded in the sun but never fell. At the wedding, I picked up the one by my plate and held it as the music started.

I took the front rooms and the loom. When the cooperative's director called to say that Marcus's quilt had been chosen for the state museum, he shrugged into the phone and said it was just scraps. He told me the same thing that night, twice, while we taped boxes. He said the museum probably needed something to fill a wall. __Yet when he packed the quilt to send it, he folded it so that the little muslin tag stitched with his name lay on top, square in the center, where anyone opening the box would see it first.__ I did not mention it. I only wrote fragile on the box in my best letters, and let him think I had not noticed.

Forty-one letters, two rubber bands, one shoebox: that was what Ama carried into the empty classroom at the language school in Accra where she now taught French in the evenings. Our mother had written them to me, Seun, during my six years at university abroad, and Ama had kept them after the funeral. We read them at a student's desk under the buzzing tube light. In every letter our mother praised my examinations. In almost every letter, near the end, she mentioned in passing that Ama had taken another shift at the market, or had postponed her own course for another year. I had read those lines at the time and skimmed past them. Now Ama read them aloud in an even voice, smoothing each page flat, and when she reached the one about the year she gave up her scholarship, she only said that the handwriting was very neat that month. I could not look at her, and I could not look away.

Folding chairs in rows on the gymnasium floor,
the Lima heat pressing through the high windows,
and I in my borrowed white, braced
for Renata, Santiago's mother,
who had said, the week before, that I was too young
to know what I was promising.
I had rehearsed my answers to her like a debate.
But when the sound system shrieked and died
and the aunts began to murmur,
it was Renata who climbed onto a bench,
her good shoes in one hand,
and sang the first hymn without a microphone
until the whole room followed.
Later she pinned my slipping veil
with a clip from her own hair
and told me, gruffly, that she had been too young once, too.
I keep that clip in a dish by the door.
I still do not know all her reasons.
I know whose voice filled the room
when mine would not come.

Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward Renata?

Why did I never ask Amelie for the scissors back? Her uncle's tailoring shop on Chicago's South Side had a back room that smelled of steam and chalk, and that was where she first lent me the brass-handled shears, the summer my family moved onto her block. I was Colby, the new boy who cut paper stars badly, and she said a good tool would fix my hands. It did not, but I kept the shears through two more moves and a decade of silence between us. Each time I unpacked them, I meant to write to her. Instead I would oil the hinge, test the blades on a scrap of newsprint, and set them back in their drawer as if they were still on loan. Last spring a cousin mentioned that Amelie now runs the shop herself. I bought a card that week; it is still blank, propped against the window above my desk.

Zhiming, the master carpenter, repeated the rule so often that Yuto came to think of it as weather, something simply true. Then came the dry summer, when the river below the village shrank to a bed of pale stones, and the farmers asked for a footbridge before the harvest. Yuto expected his master to refuse. falling into a pot? Soren did,
old captain, on the promenade bench,
explaining his fish stew to the gulls

the morning after a storm.

learning the way he tilts his wrist,
the pause he takes before the pepper,
as if the recipe were a weather
only the body could forecast.

and writes nothing on it either.

problem.passage:
Who keeps a ledger in a post office drawer?
Jens did, my uncle, behind the scale and stamps
of the little office on the edge of Rotterdam,
counting the guilders I owed him in neat blue columns
while the polder wind rattled the shutters.
For six years we traded only weather:
rain on the dikes, frost on the canal.
Then, this morning, he slid the ledger across the counter
and tore out the page that bore my name.
"Anneke," he said, "I was keeping the wrong account."
Now the stamps look softer in the window light,
and the brass scale, for once, weighs nothing at all.

Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the poem?

problem.passage:
Four rules governed my night shifts: chart every hour, never promise, never argue, and never carry food from the noodle stall by the Bergen harbor into the ward. I broke the last one for Ingrid. She had refused the hospital trays for a week and refused, too, the operation the surgeons kept urging. I did not argue; I only set the paper carton on her table and talked about the fishermen who queued at the stall at two in the morning. She ate slowly and asked about the cook, the steam, the rain drumming on the awning. Near dawn she stopped asking. She held the empty carton a long time and said, almost to herself, "Saga, I would like to see that stall in summer." When the surgeon came at seven, she signed the form.

Clove smoke and diesel drifted through the half-open window as the train pulled out of Surabaya. Arisa, retired from the bench for a decade, sat upright with her cane across her knees. Across from her, Anh, who had once clerked in her courtroom, pretended to read a newspaper. Neither mentioned the summer, years earlier, when Arisa had quietly paid his mother's hospital bills, or the careful ruling Anh had later drafted that saved Arisa's reputation. Instead they spoke of rice prices and the heat. Yet when the vendor came through, Anh paid for both their teas before she could reach her purse, and Arisa, who never let anyone pay for her, allowed it. At the next station she slipped a folded note into his newspaper without a word.

He said that at that booth, decades earlier, men who answered in French were sent to the back of the line, and that no law had ever said so. __The booth had been empty for years by then, its window boarded and its gate rusted open.__ Still, every driver in our parish slowed there, and still my grandfather spoke English. Now, when I, Odessa, drive that road alone, I catch myself doing the same.

problem.passage:
Who would believe that a schoolteacher had bound the book herself? Pearl had asked herself this all week, standing among the glue pots and cracked leather of the Kingston workshop where Hortense, her most wary student, apprenticed after lessons. The plan was simple and slightly dishonest: Pearl would tell the school board that Hortense's poems had been accepted by a press, and the handsome volume on the table would be the proof. Hortense stitched the last signature without looking up. "And when they ask for the press's name, Miss?" she said. Pearl had no answer. Hortense's hands moved steadily and exactly; Pearl's kept smoothing a page that was already flat. The lie, it seemed, would need the girl's honesty to survive, and the girl had never agreed to lend it.
